questions.question: Outline the composition of dry air, explain what separates permanent gases from variable components, and give the function of any three components.
questions.expected_answer: Dry air by volume is about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 0,93% argon and roughly 0,04% carbon dioxide, plus traces of neon, helium, methane and hydrogen. The permanent gases — nitrogen, oxygen and argon — keep effectively the same proportions everywhere in the lower atmosphere, whether sampled over Musina or over the open Atlantic. Variable components change with place and time: water vapour ranges from almost nothing over Sutherland in winter to nearly 4% over Richards Bay in summer, aerosols such as veld-fire smoke, sea salt and mine dust rise and fall with season, and ozone concentrates in the stratosphere. Functions, any three: nitrogen dilutes oxygen so burning stays manageable and supplies the stock that soil bacteria fix into nitrates for plant protein; oxygen sustains respiration and all combustion; carbon dioxide feeds photosynthesis and is a principal greenhouse gas despite its tiny share; water vapour produces all cloud and rain, carries latent heat and is the most abundant greenhouse gas; aerosols act as condensation nuclei without which cloud droplets struggle to form.

questions.question: Contrast the temperature behaviour of the troposphere and the stratosphere, giving the reason for each pattern and its consequence for weather and for aviation.
questions.expected_answer: The troposphere cools with height, at an average lapse rate of 6,5 °C per 1 000 m, because it is heated from below: the ground absorbs solar radiation and re-radiates long-wave energy, so air furthest from that source is coldest — which is why high peaks like Thabana Ntlenyana can hold sleet while nearby valleys are warm. Warm air lying under cold air is unstable, so air rises, cools and condenses, and every weather event occurs in this layer. The stratosphere warms with height because ozone between about 20 and 30 km absorbs ultraviolet radiation and releases it as heat, putting warm air on top of cool air — a standing inversion. That shuts down convection: no rising currents, almost no water vapour, no cloud and no weather. The consequence for aviation is that long-haul aircraft deliberately cruise in the lower stratosphere, above every storm, where the air is smooth and stable.

questions.question: Trace the chain from a leaking CFC appliance to a thinner ozone layer, name two consequences that matter particularly to South Africa, and assess how the world responded.
questions.expected_answer: CFCs escaped for decades from fridges, air-conditioners, aerosol cans, foams and solvents. They are chemically stable, so rain cannot wash them out and surface chemistry cannot break them; they drift upward for years until stratospheric ultraviolet cracks them apart and frees chlorine. Chlorine destroys ozone catalytically — the atom emerges from each reaction unchanged and attacks again, so a single atom can wreck tens of thousands of ozone molecules. Each southern spring the depletion concentrates over Antarctica, where the winter polar vortex isolates the air and ice-crystal clouds speed the chlorine chemistry. Two consequences for South Africa: the country lies near that thinning under already fierce sunshine, so extra ultraviolet-B raises skin cancer, cataract and immune-suppression risks in a population with skin-cancer rates among the world's highest; and ultraviolet damage to phytoplankton weakens the base of the marine food web supporting the snoek and sardine fisheries off the Atlantic coast. The response was the Montreal Protocol of 1987, which phased out CFC production internationally; measurements show the layer slowly recovering, making it the clearest success in international environmental law, though household care with old refrigerant appliances and personal sun protection remain necessary while healing continues.
